CMP1005M - Operating Systems 10 Module Overview • A morpheme is minimal meaning-bearing unit in a language, and morphology=the study of morphemes. • Examples: ❑Fox: consists of one morpheme (fox) ❑Cats: consists of two morphemes (cat, -s) • Classes of morphemes: • Roots: The central word supplying the meaning • Affixes: They add additional meaning • Example 1: worked => root=work, affix=ed • Example 2: glasses => root=glass, affix=es Parts of Words: Morphemes

CMP1005M - Operating Systems 13 Module Overview • Tokenization is the first stage of natural language processing, is the process of segmenting the running input text into tokens—for standardization purposes. • Words, morphemes and characters are three candidates for tokens. But they all have limitations. ❑ Words and morphemes seem approximately at the right level for NLP processing, but they are challenging to define and to work with in practice. ❑ Characters are clearer to define, but are too small as a unit for tokens. Subword Tokenization

CMP1005M - Operating Systems 14 Module Overview Two widely used algorithms: • Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)† • Unigram Language Modeling (ULM)‡ Stages in BPE: 1. Training: Iteratively merges frequent neigbouring tokens to create longer and longer tokens. 2. Encoder: It is used to tokenize a test sentence. Tokenization Algorithms † Sennrich, et al. “Neural machine translation of rare words with subword units”. ACL, 2016. ‡ Kudo, et al. “Subword regularization: Improving neural network translation models with multiple subword candidates”. ACL, 2018.

What is AI? AI is both science and engineering: • The science of understanding intelligent agents – explain and predict behaviors of entities • The engineering of intelligent entities 708021

Thinking Humanly: Cognitive modeling. "Machines with minds" Thinking Rationally: logical approaches “Socrates is a man; all men are mortal; therefore, Socrates is mortal." Acting Humanly: The Turing T est Acting Rationally: rational agents Four views of AI inputs rational actions 708021
Acting Humanly • When can we consider a machine to be intelligent? • Alan Turing • "Imitation Game" 1950 (picture of Alan Turing from 1951) 708021
~75% of the staff at Bletchley park were women. (Dorothy Du Boisson and Elsie Booker at Bletchley Park) 708021

Thinking Humanly Three possible routes: • introspection — we figure it out ourselves! • experiment — draw upon techniques of psychology to conduct controlled experiments. • observation — draw upon neuroscience to figure out the structure of the brain, then try to replicate it. The discipline of cognitive science: still influential in areas like human -robot interaction, explainability and some research into vision and natural language processing. Understanding how the mind works — how do we think? 708021

Thinking Rationally • Use logic to capture the laws of rational thought as symbols. • Reasoning involves shifting symbols according to well -defined rules (like algebra). • Result is idealised reasoning. • Logicist approach is theoretically attractive. How should we think? 708021

Acting Rationally • An agent is a system that perceives and acts; intelligent agent is one that acts rationally w.r.t. the goals we delegate to it. • Emphasis shifts from designing theoretically best decision -making procedure to best decision-making procedure possible in circumstances. • Logic may be used in the service of finding the best action — not an end in itself • Achieving perfect rationality — making the best decision theoretically possible — is not usually possible, due to limited resources (time, computational power, memory, uncertainty). Acting to achieve one’s goals, given one’s beliefs. 708021

Fully observable vs partially observable • Fully observable environment (aka accessible): the agent can obtain complete, accurate, up- to-date information about the environment’s state. • Most moderately complex environmentsare only partially observable (aka non-accessible). The more observable an environment is, the simpler it is tobuild agents to operate in it

Deterministic vs non-deterministic • A deterministic environment is one in which any action has a single guaranteed effect — there is no uncertainty about the state that will result from performing an action. • The physical world can to all intents and purposes be regarded as non-deterministic. • R & N calls non-deterministic environments stochastic if we quantify the non-determinism using probability theory. • Non-deterministic environments present greater problems for the agent designer.

Episodic vs sequential • Episodic environment: the performance of an agent is dependent on a number of discrete episodes, with no link between the performance of an agent in different scenarios. • Assembly line where an agent had to spot defective parts. • Episodic environments are simpler from the agent developer’s perspective because the agent can decide what action to perform based only on the current episode — it need not reason about the interactions between this and future episodes. • Non-episodic or sequential: the current decision affects future decisions. • Driving a car is sequential.

Static vs dynamic • A static environment is one that can be assumed to remain unchanged except by the performance of actions by the agent. • If the environment changes while the agent is deliberating, then it is dynamic. • A dynamic environment is one that has other processes operating on it, and which hence changes in ways beyond the agent’s control. • The physical world is a highly dynamic environment. • One reason an environment may be dynamic is the presence of other agents

Discrete vs continuous • An environment is discrete if there are a fixed, finite number of actions and percepts in it. • R & N gives a chess game as an example of a discrete environment, and taxi driving as an example of a continuous one.

Breadth first search

Breadth first search BFS Exploration Method BFS explores all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next -- uses a queue. Completeness and Optimality BFS is complete* and guarantees the shortest path if all actions have equal cost. Memory Usage and Limitations BFS requires significant memory to store all nodes at the current level, limiting its use for large state spaces. Practical Applications BFS is preferable when shortest path is essential and available memory is sufficient. *is guaranteed to find a solution if one exists (copilot, 2025)

Depth first search

Depth first Search DFS Exploration Method DFS explores each branch to its maximum depth before backtracking using a stack or recursion. Completeness and Optimality DFS is not guaranteed to find a solution if one exists. If it finds a solution, it may not be the optimal solution. Memory Efficiency DFS requires memory only for the current path and unexplored sibling nodes, making it memory-efficient. Practical Applications DFS is useful in memory-limited scenarios and when solutions are deep within the search tree. (copilot, 2025)

Breadth and depth first search Breadth-first search gives us optimality and completeness But uses a large amount of memory. Depth-first search uses less memory, but incomplete and has no guarantee of optimality. Depending on the applications, we may know roughly how deep the solution is.
Depth-limited search

Depth-limited search Depth Limit Concept DLS modifies DFS by adding a depth limit. When the depth limit is reached, DLS returns a cutoff signal instead of continuing the search further. Completeness and Optimality Not complete as the solution may be deeper than the limit. Not optimal. Memory Efficiency DLS retains DFS memory efficiency. Practical Use Cases DLS is useful when solution depth is known or estimated. (copilot, 2025)
Iterative deepening search

Iterative deepening search Depth Limit Concept IDS combines the space efficiency of DFS with the completeness of BFS by repeatedly performing DFS with increasing depth limits. Completeness and Optimality IDS is complete and finds the shortest path to the goal if all actions have equal cost, like BFS. Memory Efficiency IDS uses memory proportional to the depth limit, making it highly memory-efficient for large search spaces. Practical Use Cases IDS is ideal when the solution depth is unknown and memory resources are limited, such as in puzzle solving or pathfinding in large graphs. Might take more time than BFS but saves a lot of memory.​ (copilot, 2025)

Iterative deepening search Example: branching factor = 10 and solution depth = 5. Breadth first search: • examines 111, 111 nodes • memory requirement of 100, 000 nodes. Iterative deepening: • examines 123, 456 nodes • memory requirement of 50 nodes. Takes 11% longer in this case. Uses 2000 times less memory.
